Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood, I'm the account exec on this. We'll do a ~30-40 minute walkthrough of our hosted API for chat and text generation basics, show streaming, key params, and then Omar will do a quick demo of a couple calls.
[00:12] Maya: Thanks Lena. Quick note — Carlos and Priya are in the room, they'll ask more infra/security questions. We're primarily evaluating hosted first, likely pilot, then look at Dedicated or Private depending on results.
[00:22] Carlos: Hi all. Main constraints are latency under 200ms P50 for short queries, and cost per 1M tokens needs to be predictable. Also SOC2 + SSO are mandatory.
[00:30] Lena: Got it. We'll cover SSO and SOC2 at a high level and share the compliance pack after. Omar, take it away?
[00:36] Omar: Cool, thanks. Quick agenda: 1) API basics and request/response, 2) streaming responses and handling partials, 3) key params — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop, 4) retries and idempotency, 5) tips for cost/latency tuning, and 6) Q/A.
[00:50] Omar: So first, the API endpoint for hosted is a simple REST POST. You send a chat object or text prompt, model selection, and parameters. Example in curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -d '{"model":"rwd-3b-chat", "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the patient note"}] }'
[01:10] Maya: Quick question — do we need to handle streaming specially on mobile?
[01:14] Omar: Streaming is standard server-sent events; you can stream on mobile via typical SSE or web sockets. We return delta tokens and chunked JSON. Common pattern: render as tokens arrive and assembly on the client. Caveat: make sure your client supports reconnects.
[01:27] Priya: Does streaming affect billing?
[01:30] Omar: No, billing is per token generated/consumed — streaming is just a delivery method.
[01:34] Carlos: How about partial tokens on retries? If a request times out mid-stream, how do we handle duplicates?
[01:40] Omar: Good question. We recommend using request_id/idempotency keys. If you retry, you can send the same idempotency key and we will dedupe or return an error if it was already processed. For streaming, if the connection dropped, you can either continue by requesting the next segment, or re-request with same idempotency key — the server will handle. Also note some model variants have session/KV cache semantics that make exact dedupe hard, so we recommend deterministic prompts for critical operations.
[02:05] Maya: When you say KV cache, you mean the attention key-value cache for speedups, right?
[02:09] Omar: Exactly, the KV cache we maintain per session to avoid re-computing previous tokens when the conversation continues. It reduces latency for follow-ups. For hosted we manage it transparently; for Dedicated/Private there are config knobs.
[02:20] Lena: Quick demo time — Omar will show a live chat call and then a streaming example.
[02:25] Omar: Ok, I'm sharing my screen. First non-streaming: POST chat, get full response. Now streaming: I send the same prompt but add "stream":true and I get a series of events: data: {"delta":"Hello"} ... and final event with role/content and usage.
[03:05] Omar: Note the usage object contains token counts for prompt and completion — useful for cost analysis. Also we return model and model_version so you can tie costs to model choices.
[03:22] Maya: How do we choose model sizes? We have constraints — smaller models for low-latency assistant tasks, larger ones for creative summarization.
[03:30] Omar: Right. Our catalog lists performance profiles; e.g., rwd-3b-chat is fast and cheap, rwd-13b is higher quality but higher latency/cost. We provide recommended defaults by workload. We can run a small benchmark with your representative prompts.
[03:42] Carlos: Is there any auto-fallback if a model is saturated? We want predictable latency.
[03:47] Omar: Hosted can route by policy: latency-first or cost-first. If your primary model is saturated, we can fallback to a compatible variant or queue with a capacity tier. For stricter SLAs you'd move to Dedicated.
[03:58] Priya: How does rate limiting look? We need burst control for spikes.
[04:02] Omar: We expose per-key rate limits and burst windows. For hosted, default limits are moderate but can be raised for pilots. We also provide an error code schema: 429 for rate limit, 503 for transient capacity issues. For retries we suggest exponential backoff with jitter.
[04:20] Omar: Typical retry pattern: on 429/503, backoff 500ms -> 1s -> 2s, apply jitter, cap at 8-10s. For idempotent writes you can retry safe, for non-idempotent you must guard with idempotency keys.
[04:34] Maya: Any examples for SDKs?
[04:36] Omar: Yes, we have Python, Node, and curl examples. I'll paste sample code after the call; it includes streaming handlers and reconnect examples.
[04:45] Carlos: Security — where do logs and data live, do you retain customer data?
[04:50] Lena: For hosted, we default to short retention for logs and offer a data retention policy per account. We support encryption at rest, TLS in transit, and KMS integration for key management. SOC 2 cert info will be shared; we also have options for disabling retention for PII-sensitive flows.
[05:06] Priya: Do you support SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning?
[05:09] Lena: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM-provisioning and RBAC integration. We'll send our security pack which includes architecture diagrams and details.
[05:16] Maya: For the pilot we want to measure token cost and latency. What sample rate do you recommend for synthetic benchmarking?
[05:22] Omar: Use 1k–5k representative prompts and run over 3 different models. We'll provide a small harness. Measure P50/P95 latency including network time, and tokens per call to estimate cost. We'll also suggest batching strategies if you have high throughput non-interactive inference.
[05:36] Carlos: You mentioned batching — how does batching interact with streaming?
[05:40] Omar: Streaming is primarily per-request; batching is for throughput-oriented workloads where you send many inputs in one request. It's incompatible with token-level streaming; you'd get the batched output once. Use streaming for interactive low-latency UX, batching for high throughput offline jobs.
[05:56] Maya: Any advice for temperature/top_p tuning?
[05:59] Omar: For deterministic summaries keep temperature near 0.0 and top_p small. For creative outputs set temperature 0.7 and top_p 0.9. Also use stop sequences where appropriate. Increase max_tokens cautiously — more tokens = more cost.
[06:15] Priya: Are there server-side defaults we can override?
[06:18] Omar: Yes defaults are set per account and per route; you can override at call-time in the request. Redwood Optimize can also suggest per-route param presets based on your prompt sets.
[06:30] Maya: If we hit a model regression after a rollout, can we rollback easily?
[06:34] Lena: Yes we support pinned model versions and can do canary rollouts. Our console shows per-route quality/regression alerts if you run evals against reference prompts.
[06:45] Carlos: Network egress/data residency — can you guarantee region placement for hosted?
[06:49] Lena: Hosted has region controls; for strict residency we recommend Private deployments. We'll map options in the security doc.
[06:58] Omar: Demo wrap-up: pasted a sample streaming handler, idempotency key pattern, and recommended retry backoff.
[07:05] Maya: This was helpful. Couple follow-ups: 1) send pricing + pilot agreement, 2) security pack, and 3) the benchmark harness.
[07:14] Lena: Yep on it. Any final questions?
[07:18] Priya: Could we get a sample of the usage object schema?
[07:21] Omar: Yes, I'll include the exact response schema in the follow-up. It includes prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens and model_version.
[07:29] Carlos: Also, can you share your SLOs/uptime for hosted?
[07:33] Lena: Hosted has published SLOs; Dedicated has SLA options. We'll include the SLO doc link.
[07:39] Maya: Great. Thanks Lena and Omar. We'll review materials and come back with dates for the benchmark.
[07:44] Lena: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the artifacts.
[07:48] (call ends)
